Full pre-registration sweep: NOT READY — 3 BLOCKING findings.

Counts by severity: BLOCKING=3 / NON-BLOCKING HYGIENE=0 / SUGGESTION=1
Counts by issue type: factual=0 / structural=2 / scope-related=2

What passes:
- Local table mechanics: 18 rows x 5 columns; exactly three rows per continent; List Position values are 1-3 inside each continent; duplicate count for primary_key=(Continent, Language) is 0; CSV header matches draft.columns; column_types cover exactly the five columns; source_count=11 equals len(source_urls).
- Metadata fit in broad strokes: query_category=scaled_enumeration and operation_type=union+filter match a partitioned top-3-by-continent shape; domain=Society/Languages is appropriate; Antarctica exclusion is documented.
- Several partitions have good direct support. South America is directly supported by the Languages of South America table, which lists Portuguese 215,754,600, Spanish 214,265,000, and Quechua 7,735,620 above the next language (staged ground-truth source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Languages_of_South_America, Main languages table, lines 129-141). Europe rows are supported by the Languages of Europe article/table for Russian, German, and French counts/families (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Languages_of_Europe, Russian discussion/table and German/French rows, lines 298, 518, 525, 599). Africa row values are at least individually supported: Languages of Africa lists Arabic at 150M L1 and Hausa/Yoruba are supported by cited language pages (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Languages_of_Africa, demographics table, lines 569-571, 605, 753, 1154; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausa_language, infobox, lines 264-279; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoruba_language, infobox, lines 232-242).

Findings:

1. (structural, BLOCKING) North America numeric values are derived from uncited sources, not supported by the staged URL set.

The North America source supports the rank order English > Spanish > French, but it does not provide the staged L1 counts (~270, ~165, ~10). It says English, Spanish, and French are the most widely spoken languages, and repeats that English is followed by Spanish and French, but gives no numeric L1 table (staged ground-truth source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Languages_of_North_America, lead / Introduced languages, lines 117-119 and 132-134). The curation notes say the counts were derived from per-language country breakdowns, but the staged source_urls do not include the English, Spanish, or French language pages, nor census sources for the US/Canada/Mexico/Caribbean calculations. Local locators: datasets/pkdb_bench/staging/top3_languages_per_continent.csv lines 11-13; draft.json source_urls lines 31-42; curation.json source_coverage_notes source_urls[4].

This violates the row-value source contract: L1 Speakers (M) is an evaluated column, and every row/value must trace to a cited URL. The tilde notation honestly signals approximation, but it does not substitute for citing the load-bearing derivation sources.

Minimal repair: add the exact per-language/per-country sources used for the North America calculations to source_urls, update source_count and Roles, or remove the numeric North America values / change the column to a nonnumeric qualitative rank label for rows whose cited source only supports ordering.

2. (scope-related, BLOCKING) The Oceania top-3 row universe is not source-defined by the cited sources.

The table title commits to the three most widely spoken languages by native/L1 speakers per inhabited continent. For Oceania, the cited Languages of Oceania page is a short overview that lists language groups and examples; it names English, French, Hindi, Tok Pisin, other creoles, and Fiji Hindi, but it does not give a continent-restricted L1 ranking or counts (staged ground-truth source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Languages_of_Oceania, overview and non-indigenous/creole-language list, lines 136-150). The Tok Pisin and Fiji Hindi pages support those two selected languages' L1 counts and families individually (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tok_Pisin, infobox, lines 212-221; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiji_Hindi, infobox, lines 222-232), but they do not establish that these are the #2 and #3 languages across Oceania by L1. The curation record itself calls the Oceania #2/#3 picks debatable and describes them as article-emphasis/curator choices rather than a source-defined ranking. Local locators: curation.json source_coverage_notes source_urls[6], decision_log Further decisions item 8, open_questions item 7.

This materially affects the row universe. A model answering the natural-language query could reasonably choose French, Hindi/Fiji Hindi, Tok Pisin, or other large regional languages depending on L1 vs total speaker treatment, and the current cited source set does not define which top three are ground truth.

Minimal repair: either add a reliable source that actually ranks/counts Oceania languages by L1 and rebuild rows to match it, or retitle/reframe the Oceania partition as a selected illustrative set rather than source_defined top-3. If keeping a source_defined top-3 claim, the row universe needs a systematic source, not two selected language pages plus a mention-only overview.

3. (structural, BLOCKING) The Oceania List Position values contradict the staged L1 counts.

Within Oceania, Tok Pisin is position 2 with ~0.12M L1 speakers, while Fijian Hindi is position 3 with ~0.34M L1 speakers. The cited per-language pages support the same relative order problem: Tok Pisin has 130,000 native speakers, while Fiji Hindi has 380,000 native speakers (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tok_Pisin, infobox, lines 214-217; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiji_Hindi, infobox, lines 225-227). Local locator: datasets/pkdb_bench/staging/top3_languages_per_continent.csv lines 14-16.

Because the title and decision_log define List Position as the rank by L1/native speakers, the row order should not place the lower-L1 language ahead of the higher-L1 language. This is independent of the broader Oceania row-universe blocker above.

Minimal repair: if both languages remain after a source-defined Oceania rebuild, swap Fijian Hindi ahead of Tok Pisin or explicitly drop ranking semantics from List Position and the title. For the current title, reorder by the cited L1 counts.

4. (scope-related, SUGGESTION) The source_defined claim is fragile for a mixed-source, mixed-convention top-3 table.

Some partitions are close to source-defined (South America, Europe). Others depend on cross-source manual comparison, derived continent-restricted approximations, or selected-language pages. This mixed construction can still become registration-ready, but only if the source plan explicitly supplies the load-bearing sources for each partition and the title/db_analog honestly describes the ranking rule. Local locator: curation.json claim_type and source_coverage_notes. Wiki-family discovery did not surface one clean direct Wikipedia page for “top three L1 languages by continent”; the current repair path is likely source-plan expansion plus narrower wording, not a single-source swap.

Minimal cleanup: after fixing the blockers, add an audit_response.cycle_1 explaining whether the repaired table remains source_defined or becomes partially_supplemented, and document per-partition ranking evidence separately from per-row value evidence.

Final judgment: Not ready. The CSV mechanics are clean, but the current source set does not support enough of the evaluated top-3/L1 contract, especially for North America and Oceania.

Minimal fixes needed:
1. Add cited sources for the North America L1 count derivations, or remove/reframe those numeric cells.
2. Rebuild Oceania from a source that defines an L1 top-three ranking, or reframe it as a selected illustrative set.
3. Fix Oceania List Position ordering if Tok Pisin and Fijian Hindi remain.
4. Reassess claim_type/source_defined after the mixed-source repairs.
5. Append audit_response.cycle_1 and rerun preflight.
